https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cy4k.text: Image source, Reuters Image caption, Former Pakistani Prime Minister Imran Khan has been jailed since 2023 By Olivia Ireland Published 2 hours ago Pakistan's Supreme Court has ordered jailed former Prime Minister Imran Khan to be moved to hospital, following complaints about his poor health. A three-judge panel ordered that the cricketer-turned-politician be taken to Shifa International Hospital in Islamabad in the next 48 hours to be examined by physicians. The court also said Khan would be allowed weekly meetings with family members and telephone calls with his sons. Khan has been imprisoned since 2023 on corruption charges, which he says were politically motivated. The Pakistani government has not publicly commented on the court ruling. In Tuesday's court order, the panel wrote: "We are mindful of the constitutional and legal obligation... to safeguard the life, health, dignity and security of the prisoner." The 73-year-old's lawyers have said he's suffering from various health conditions, including poor eyesight, and has been unable to access specialist medical care. In February, Khan's lawyer said his client had 15% vision left in his right eye after prison authorities failed to take action - an allegation the government disputed. Reacting to the ruling, Zulfikar Bukhari, an adviser to Khan, said in quotes cited by AFP news agency: "We wish it had happened sooner so his eye and general health would not have deteriorated this much". The court order said an eye specialist would be involved in Khan's hospital treatment. The judges and members of Khan's political party, Tehreek-e-Insaf, have warned supporters not to gather outside the hospital when he is transferred there, which would be a breach of the court order. Khan, who previously captained the Pakistan national cricket team, served as the country's prime minister from 2018 to 2022. He was imprisoned in August 2023 and has faced charges in more than 100 cases, ranging from leaking state secrets to selling state gifts - all of which he decried as politically motivated. Khan and his wife Bushra Bibi were both sentenced to 17 years late last year. His jailing triggered large-scale protests by supporters, which were met with a crackdown by authorities. Despite his jailing, Khan remains a significant presence in Pakistani politics with a large number of supporters. World By CNN Newsource Published October 13, 2026 9:00 PM By Billy Stockwell, CNN (CNN) — It started with a stream of bubbles rising to the surface of the Baltic Sea. Seven months after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, explosions burst through two Nord Stream gas pipelines – Russia’s controversial gas highway into Europe – in the waters between Sweden and Poland. Investigators from several countries raced to determine who was responsible and fingers were immediately pointed at Russia. Then, two Ukrainian nationals were arrested, raising questions about state involvement and presenting a test of loyalty for some of Kyiv’s European allies. On Wednesday, one of them will go on trial in Germany accused of involvement in one of the biggest – and most mysterious – acts of sabotage in modern history. He denies wrongdoing and Ukraine has denied any involvement. Here’s what you need to know: What is Nord Stream and what happened? Nord Stream 1 and 2 are two major conduits created to funnel Russian gas to Europe, via Germany. Owned by Nord Stream AG, whose majority shareholder is the Russian gas firm Gazprom, the pipelines were divisive even before the start of the Ukraine war, mainly due to concerns over European reliance on cheap Russian hydrocarbons. Nord Stream 1 was announced in 1997, when relations between the West and post-Soviet Russia were relatively calm, and became operational in 2011. Nord Stream 2, a sister project, was completed in September 2021, but never entered service. Germany shelved it days before Moscow invaded Ukraine. In late September 2022, explosions ripped through the two pipelines near the Danish island of Bornholm, releasing plumes of gas into the surrounding water and sparking a cross-border investigation. How did the investigation unfold? Sweden was the first country to sound the alarm on the leaks. Some experts at the time said they could have been caused by a technical malfunction, but the leaders of several Western countries were quick to identify sabotage as the likely cause. Two months after the event, Swedish prosecutors announced the incident was a result of “gross sabotage,” adding that “traces of explosives” had been found at the scene. Although neither pipeline was in operation at the time of the attack, both still contained gas under pressure. As a result, experts said an “unprecedented” amount of the greenhouse gases might have leaked into the atmosphere. Several agencies were tasked with digging into the attack, including German, Danish and Scandinavian security authorities. European officials vowed a firm response. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said any deliberate act to disrupt Europe’s energy infrastructure was “unacceptable” and would “lead to the strongest response possible.” Germany in particular was keen to see the alleged culprits brought to justice and, in 2024, authorities there issued an international arrest warrant for a Ukrainian man suspected of involvement. Since then, two Ukrainian men have been arrested over their alleged role in the pipeline attacks. Denmark and Sweden both closed their criminal investigations into the explosions in 2024, with Sweden citing a lack of jurisdiction and Denmark saying there were not sufficient grounds to pursue the case. This left Berlin the only nation to pursue the leads. Who is on trial? Serhii Kuznietsov, a former Ukrainian soldier , is the lone defendant in the trial starting Wednesday in Hamburg, where he is identified only as Serhii K under German privacy laws. German prosecutors said he “belongs to a group of people who planted explosive devices in the gas pipelines Nord Stream 1 and Nord Stream 2 near the island of Bornholm in September 2022.” Prosecutors have accused Serhii K of being an accomplice to the “war crime” of attacking civilian objects, destruction of infrastructure, causing an explosion and disrupting public operations, according to court filings. The court filings accused him of “acting on behalf of Ukrainian state authorities” in an alleged plot to destroy the Nord Stream pipelines. His defense lawyer previously told CNN that he denies any wrongdoing. In 2025, Kuznietsov was arrested by Italian police in Rimini – a city in northern Italy known for its sandy beaches and Roman landmarks – and later extradited to Germany. Prosecutors in Germany believe he and his accomplices used a sailing yacht to carry out the attack, traveling from the port of Rostock, a city in northern Germany. The vessel had been rented from a German company via intermediaries using forged identity documents, prosecutors claim. The second Ukrainian man arrested in connection with the bombing, Volodymyr Zhuravlov, was detained in August in Croatia, where a court has approved his extradition to Germany, Reuters reported last month. His lawyer dismissed the ruling and said he could appeal the decision, Reuters added. German prosecutors said he was “strongly suspected” of several criminal offenses, including sabotage and causing an explosion, and participating in dives to the pipelines. Zhuravlov was previously arrested in Poland, which declined to extradite him to Germany. How does this link to the wider war? The explosions rang out at a tense time for Europe. The attacks heightened the controversy over Europe’s use of Russian gas and put Germany – the driving force behind the gas project – under the spotlight over former chancellor Angela Merkel’s decision to adopt a conciliatory approach to Moscow despite its recent aggression toward Ukraine and Georgia. Donald Tusk, the prime minister of Ukraine’s close ally Poland, said last year that Europe’s problem was “not that Nord Stream 2 was blown up, but that it was built.” As far back as 2007, Poland’s then-defense minister Radek Sikorski railed against the Nord Stream 1 pipeline, then under construction, calling it “the most outrageous attempt by Mr Putin to divide and damage the EU.” When Zhuravlov was initially arrested in Poland, a judge ruled against his extradition to Germany, saying that if the Nord Stream blasts were an act of Ukrainian sabotage, it would be a justified response to an unprovoked invasion. With court officials saying Wednesday’s trial is expected to run until February next year, Germany will be hoping no new roadblocks lie ahead as it seeks to get to the truth of this murky affair. https://24.hu/kulfold/2026/11/11/oroszor.text: Folytatódtak Abu-Dzabiban az orosz–ukrán háborút érintő béketárgyalások – írja a Reuters . Oroszország főtárgyalója, Vlagyimir Megyinszkij a szerdai tárgyalásokat követően elmondta, hogy voltak olyan témák, melyeket hasonlóan láttak az ukránokkal. Azt is elmondta, hogy a kétnapos egyeztetések legkiemelkedőbb témája egy lehetséges új, európai védelmi keretrendszer volt. Az amerikai féllel egyetemesen eszmecserét folytattunk erről a témáról is. Néhány ponton egyetértettünk, másokban nem, de a tárgyalások folytatódnak. A világnak szüksége van egy új, modern védelmi rendszerre, olyanra, amely nem helyez bizonyos országokat hátrányos helyzetbe – nyilatkozta Megyinszkij az orosz állami televíziónak. Európa lehetséges csatlakozását a tárgyalásokhoz azonban hűvösen fogadta a főtárgyaló. Szerinte az EU-nak és Oroszországnak nincs miről tárgyalnia, hisz állítása szerint az Unió sosem próbált nyitni feléjük. Azt mondta, az amerikaiaktól érdemes lenne tanulnia az Uniónak józan ész, realizmus és békevágy tekintetében is. Megyinszkij hozzátette, hogy nagy fokú túszcserében is megegyeztek a felek a béketárgyalásoknak köszönhetően.

https://www.dw.com/en/uk-court-convicts-.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5PNr5 Prefer DW on Google The trial opened at Woolwich Crown Court in London on October 5 this year Image: Kin Cheung/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement Two Iranian men were found guilty of spying on dissident journalists in Britain on behalf of Iran's Revolutionary Guard on Thursday. British counterterrorism police said the case reflected intensifying hostile Iranian activity in the country, an issue that recently made headlines amid the security scare at the RAF Fairford airbase that's a major operational site in Europe for the US Air Force. The men, both in their 40s, were arrested last year, with Iran repeatedly rejecting the allegations against them. What did the court rule? The Woolwich Crown Court in London convicted one of the Iranian citizens not just of spying on journalists working for the Persian-language dissident TV channel Iran International, but of plotting a violent attack against one or more of them. The second individual had also faced charges of plotting an attack but was only convicted of spying on the reporters. One of the convicted defendants said he was acting under duress after his family was threatened, and the other said he did not know that his actions were assisting Iranian intelligence. A third defendant, a 57-year-old Iranian man, was acquitted of all charges. Sentencing in the case is expected at the 'Old Bailey' in London on December 17 Image: Kin Cheung/AP Photo/picture alliance The men were accused of engaging in conduct likely to assist the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), Iran's multi-discipline military force that's seen as closer to the country's religious leadership and more influential than its regular armed forces. The UK formally designated the IRGC as a threat to national security in July, meaning that supporting or assisting the organization can carry penalties of up to 14 years in prison as part of new rules on national security and state threats. Sentencing in this case is still pending and is scheduled for mid-December. "This was a calculated operation to spy on those critical of the Iranian regime," said Frank Ferguson, chief prosecutor for the Crown Prosecution Service's special crime and counter-terrorism division. The two men were accused of visiting addresses linked to their targets, taking photos and videos, and using platforms such as ChatGPT to research them online "Thankfully, the defendants were stopped before any attack could take place," prosecutor Ferguson said. Senior ‌National Coordinator for Counter Terrorism Policing Vicki Evans said that the IRGC or "middlemen" for Iranian intelligence were directing the plot. Iran's government had repeatedly denied the allegations, with Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi saying he was "disturbed" by the trio's arrests last May. UK releases air base plot suspects To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Not the first plot targeting Iran International There have been four cases targeting the Persian language television channel Iran International since late 2023. In July, two Romanian men were jailed for stabbing a journalist outside his home in 2024. A spokesman for the broadcaster's parent company, Volant Media, said in a statement that Thursday's verdicts "don't make the lives of our journalists any safer so long as the Islamic Republic of Iran continues its campaign of death threats and violence against them." Iran International reported that a British barrister was also one of the targets. What other alleged signs of Iranian hostile activity in the UK are there? British law enforcement has been warning of an uptick of hostile Iranian activity in recent years, particularly since the US military operations against Tehran began earlier this year. Most notably, the UK has accused Iran of being behind a suspected plot targeting the RAF Fairford base in September , after which US President Donald Trump withdrew some long-range bombers from the site . Three men were indicted in the US in relation to that plot this week , while two others currently face charges in the UK. But beyond this, the head of Britain's MI5 domestic intelligence agency Ken MacCullum said in October that Iran-linked operations had led to more than 50 arrests in the last year. He also said known cases of so-called state threats had more than quadrupled in a decade. Counter-terrorism police chief Evans said she expected this trend to continue. France this week also accused Iran of being behind a cyberattack targeting refrigeration units at hundreds of supermarkets in October, although Iran denied any involvement. European governments are on heightened alert for so-called hybrid warfare tactics, from Russia as well as Iran, amid the geopolitical tensions of recent years. New technologies like low-cost drones and AI are also threatening to make such activities cheaper, harder to trace, and potentially more effective.
